alma-plan.welcome: Thinking about using AlmaLinux every day? Let’s first check the apps and equipment you need, then try Linux inside a practice VM before changing your main computer.
alma-plan.why: A virtual machine, or VM, is a computer running inside another computer. It lets you learn while keeping your current Windows setup in place.
needs: You’ll need a Windows computer with VMware Workstation Pro and enough spare resources for a practice VM.
For this desktop exercise, plan 2 virtual CPU cores, 4 GB of memory minimum, 8 GB if your host can spare it, and a new 50 GB virtual disk.
Have a separate backup of important Windows files and a list of everyday apps, games, printers, and other devices you use.
alma-plan.firstMove: Open your notes and list the things you use your computer for each day, such as browsing, documents, video calls, and games.
alma-plan.reassurance: You don’t need to replace Windows to take this class. We’ll first find out what works for you inside a VM.

alma-install.welcome: Let’s build your AlmaLinux practice desktop. We’ll make a new virtual computer, attach the installer, and choose the GNOME desktop so you have menus and windows to work with.
alma-install.why: Starting with a new virtual disk keeps your learning separate from the files on your real Windows drive.
needs: You’ll need VMware Workstation Pro and the desktop resource plan from the previous class.
Download the official AlmaLinux 9 x86_64 DVD ISO and its matching checksum; the ISO is the installer image we attach like a virtual DVD.
Have a new 50 GB virtual disk for ALMA-DESKTOP, with 2 virtual CPU cores and your planned memory allocation.
alma-install.firstMove: On Windows, verify the downloaded installer’s checksum before opening VMware’s File → New Virtual Machine wizard.
alma-install.reassurance: In the installer, Server with GUI is the choice that includes GNOME. Check that only the new practice disk is selected before accepting any disk changes.

alma-first-login.welcome: Welcome to your new desktop. Let’s make the screen, keyboard, sound, and lock screen comfortable, then update Linux and check the VMware guest tools.
alma-first-login.why: A few careful setup choices make your everyday computer easier to use and give us a known working starting point.
needs: You’ll need the installed ALMA-DESKTOP VM with the AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop.
Sign in using the normal user you created during installation and keep that user’s password private.
Have a working internet connection through the VM’s NAT network and save any open work before the update and restart.
alma-first-login.firstMove: Open the system menu at the top-right of GNOME and select Settings. Start with Displays so the text is easy to read.
alma-first-login.reassurance: If the picture doesn’t resize with the VMware window yet, that’s something we’ll check with the guest tools. Don’t reinstall the desktop just for that.

alma-terminal.welcome: Let’s get comfortable with the terminal one small task at a time. We’ll make a practice folder, create a tiny file, and learn how to find help when a command is unfamiliar.
alma-terminal.why: The terminal is another way to tell your computer what to do. Practicing in your own practice folder makes the results easier to understand.
needs: You’ll need your AlmaLinux GNOME desktop, signed in as your normal user.
We’ll use only a practice folder inside your home folder; no valuable files need to be changed.
Keep the class open beside Terminal so you can read one command and its explanation before trying it.
alma-terminal.firstMove: Click Activities, type Terminal, and open it. Start by checking your username and current folder.
alma-terminal.reassurance: It’s normal not to remember commands yet. Use the help examples, and press q when you need to leave a help page.

alma-files.welcome: Now let’s use both Files and the terminal to organize the practice note you made. We’ll copy it, check its permissions, and try a small archive.
alma-files.why: Learning both views helps you connect the folders you click with the paths you type in commands.
needs: You’ll need the DesktopPractice folder and notes.txt from the previous command lesson.
Use your normal AlmaLinux user and the GNOME Files app.
For the removable-storage step, use a separate USB data drive you are allowed to use; leave important files backed up elsewhere.
alma-files.firstMove: Open Activities → Files, then use Ctrl+L to enter ~/DesktopPractice and find notes.txt.
alma-files.reassurance: If the file isn’t there, check the folder first. Keep the original note and practice with copies so a wrong click is easy to undo.

alma-apps.welcome: Let’s add an everyday app and learn where it comes from. We’ll use AlmaLinux’s package tools first, then look at a user-only Flatpak app from Flathub.
alma-apps.why: Different app sources have different publishers and permissions. Checking those details helps you make a choice you understand.
needs: You’ll need an updated AlmaLinux 9 GNOME desktop with internet access.
Use your normal user and keep its administrator password private for any approved system-package changes.
Be ready to read an app’s source and permissions before accepting a third-party install.
alma-apps.firstMove: Open Activities → Terminal and check which software sources and Flatpak tools are already configured.
alma-apps.reassurance: If an app isn’t available from one source, don’t add random repositories. We’ll check the intended source and exact app name together.

alma-games.welcome: Let’s set up Steam and try one small game that your computer can actually run. After that, we’ll look at Proton, which helps some Windows games run on Linux.
alma-games.why: Game support depends on the title, graphics hardware, and sometimes anti-cheat software. A successful Steam install does not promise every game will work.
needs: You’ll need the user-scoped Flatpak and Flathub setup from the apps lesson.
Have a Steam account and a small game you own or a free native Linux title; keep sign-in and Steam Guard codes private.
Use the VM for setup practice. For playing games, check the actual computer’s graphics support and the game’s current requirements.
alma-games.firstMove: Read the chosen game’s official Linux and graphics requirements before installing or downloading it.
alma-games.reassurance: If a game doesn’t run in the VM, that may be a graphics limit rather than something you did wrong. Record the result and check the game’s support notes.

alma-network.welcome: Let’s connect the everyday things you need: your network, a printer, and an allowed file share. We’ll check what is already working before changing settings.
alma-network.why: Looking first helps us tell a network problem from a printer or name-lookup problem without changing several settings at once.
needs: You’ll need your AlmaLinux GNOME desktop and a network you are allowed to use.
For printing, have a supported printer and its confirmed name or address.
For file sharing, have the exact permitted share address and an account allowed to open it; don’t enter secrets into the class page.
alma-network.firstMove: Open Settings → Network and check the active connection. In VMware, virtual Ethernet is normal even if Windows is on Wi-Fi.
alma-network.reassurance: If the printer or Bluetooth device isn’t visible inside the VM, check whether it has been connected to the guest. Don’t reset the whole network first.

alma-wd-drive.welcome: Let’s add storage carefully and keep the files you already own. We’ll identify your Western Digital drive, open an existing volume safely, and use a separate blank practice disk for formatting lessons.
alma-wd-drive.why: A disk’s letter or Linux device name can change. Matching its model, serial number, and size helps prevent erasing the wrong drive.
needs: You’ll need a separate, checked backup of any files on the WD drive and a successful sample restore.
Know whether your drive is external USB or internal SATA, its model and serial number, and whether it already contains files to keep.
For the formatting exercise, use a new empty virtual disk. Do not give the VM raw access to your Windows system disk.
alma-wd-drive.firstMove: Open Activities → Disks and compare the candidate drive’s model, serial number, and capacity with the physical label or new virtual-disk plan.
alma-wd-drive.reassurance: If the identity is uncertain, stop before clicking Format or Delete. Existing files can be mounted without formatting, and the blank-disk exercise is optional.

alma-backup.welcome: Let’s make a backup of your everyday files and then bring one sample back. We’ll restore it into a different folder so your original stays safe.
alma-backup.why: A backup is useful when you can get the files back. A sample restore helps prove that your copy can do the job.
needs: You’ll need a separate storage device or approved backup destination with enough free space.
Keep the practice notes.txt and Everyday folder from the earlier classes.
Choose a restore-test folder in your home directory; we won’t overwrite the original files.
alma-backup.firstMove: Open Files and list the folders you would miss if this desktop stopped working, starting with your own documents and practice files.
alma-backup.reassurance: A VM snapshot is useful for a short experiment, but it isn’t a separate backup of your important files. We’ll keep those two jobs distinct.

alma-troubleshoot.welcome: Something isn’t working? Let’s slow it down and gather a few clues. We’ll check the exact error, free space, memory, and relevant service logs before choosing a fix.
alma-troubleshoot.why: Changing one thing at a time makes it easier to tell which action actually helped and how to undo it if needed.
needs: You’ll need your normal AlmaLinux terminal and notes about the last working state.
Pick a real, harmless problem to check; you do not need to break anything for this class.
Have administrator access available only when a log or check requires it, and keep SELinux and the firewall enabled.
alma-troubleshoot.firstMove: Write down what failed, when it started, the exact error, and the last change you remember.
alma-troubleshoot.reassurance: If the first check doesn’t reveal the cause, that’s okay. Keep the observation and move to the next check instead of disabling protections or restarting everything.

alma-real-terminal.welcome: Let’s connect the lesson to a real terminal on your computer. We’ll first prove that the local companion is running PowerShell on Windows, then use AlmaLinux’s own terminal or a checked SSH connection for Linux commands.
alma-real-terminal.why: The place where you type matters. Windows PowerShell, a WSL distribution, and your VMware AlmaLinux guest are different computers or environments.
needs: You’ll need your Windows computer with Git, Node.js 22.13 or later, npm, and the SONIC-Academy repository.
Have your AlmaLinux VM running and know the normal user you created inside it.
Use two local PowerShell windows for the website and companion processes; keep the pairing token private and do not publish a public tunnel.
alma-real-terminal.firstMove: On Windows, open a normal PowerShell window in the repository folder. Keep the AlmaLinux guest’s GNOME Terminal available separately.
alma-real-terminal.reassurance: If a command gives a Windows result, check the selected terminal before changing it. We’ll prove where commands run using the computer name and clock.
